paragraphs.text: Hoxha-Aliu syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by mild intellectual disability or developmental delay and distal limb anomalies. The limb anomalies include brachydactyly, clinodactyly, short or dysplastic nails, short metacarpals, and toe syndactyly (Hoxha and Aliu, 2023; Guo et al., 2023). Some patients have also had short stature, dysmorphic facial features, and cardiac malformations (Choucair et al., 2017; Szot et al., 2021).

paragraphs.text: Szot et al. (2021) described a girl (F5.II.1) with reduction defects of the hands and feet. On the right hand she had a transverse terminal limb reduction with a rudimentary fifth digit. Several digits had hypoplastic or absent nails. Toes 2 to 4 of the right foot and toes 3 to 5 of the left foot were absent, and she had syndactyly. She also had a perimembranous ventricular septal defect, pulmonary vein stenosis, microcephaly, global developmental delay, and autism. Dysmorphic features included brachycephaly with a flat occiput and bitemporal narrowing, a small nose, and cupped prominent ears. She had bilateral inguinal hernias. No vertebral or renal defects were recorded.

paragraphs.text: Choucair et al. (2017) performed chromosomal microarray analysis in a male child born to consanguineous parents and found a homozygous deletion at 8p23.1. The deletion contained the microRNA miR-4660 and the ERI1 and MFHAS1 genes. The authors noted that ERI1 is a ribonuclease involved in RNA metabolism and that it is required for correct skeletal patterning by defining HOXC8 expression. They discussed how the deleted genes might contribute to the patient's features.

paragraphs.text: Szot et al. (2021) reported patient F5.II.1, a girl with limb reduction defects, cardiac defects, microcephaly, global developmental delay, and autism. She carried a homozygous loss-of-function variant in the ERI1 gene (c.514C-T, NM_153332.4; gln172-to-ter, Q172X). She was also homozygous for a missense variant in the KYNU gene (605197) (c.616G-A; glu206-to-lys, E206K). The authors noted that ERI1 had previously been found in a homozygous microdeletion, together with MFHAS1, in a patient whose limb and cardiac abnormalities resembled hers. They suggested that the ERI1 variant may help explain her phenotype but said that the functional link between ERI1 mutation and these defects remained to be assessed.

paragraphs.text: Hoxha and Aliu (2023) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the ERI1 gene in a female patient. She had mild intellectual disability and eyelid ptosis. Her hand and foot anomalies included brachydactyly, clinodactyly, brachytelephalangy, short metacarpals, toe syndactyly, and dysplastic or short nails of the halluces.
